nameStory: The Juniper Geometer Moth gets its name from its caterpillars' love of juniper trees and their family's distinctive way of moving. Geometer moths are called "earth measurers" because their caterpillars loop their bodies as they crawl, appearing to measure the ground inch by inch like a tiny surveyor with a measuring tape.
description: The Juniper Geometer is a small, delicate moth with a wingspan of about an inch (21-25 mm). Like other geometer moths, it has a slender body and holds its wings horizontally when at rest, creating a triangular silhouette. These moths are typically earth-toned with subtle patterns that help them blend in with tree bark during the day. You'll find adults flying from spring through fall, with multiple generations each year.

idTips.label: Size and Wing Span
idTips.description: Small moth with wings spanning just under an inch, about the width of a quarter

idTips.label: Resting Position
idTips.description: Holds wings horizontally when at rest, creating a flat triangular shape against tree bark or surfaces

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender, delicate body typical of geometer moths, much thinner than chunky sphinx or tiger moths

idTips.label: Habitat Association
idTips.description: Found near juniper trees and shrubs where their caterpillars feed, often attracted to lights at night

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttery flight that seems almost hesitant compared to stronger-flying moth families

habitat: Look for Juniper Geometers in areas with native juniper trees and shrubs, including rocky hillsides, old fields, and forest edges throughout New England. They're also found around ornamental junipers in suburban areas and parks. Occasionally they'll use eastern white cedar (northern white cedar) and possibly white pine as host plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in April, often seen at porch lights and outdoor lighting. This is when the first generation starts mating and laying eggs on juniper foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple overlapping generations. Adults are commonly attracted to lights throughout summer nights, and tiny looping caterpillars may be spotted on juniper branches.
seasonality.fall: Final generation of adults continues flying into November in warmer areas. Late-season caterpillars are preparing to overwinter, becoming less active as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent, but larvae overwinter in protected spots on or near their juniper host plants, waiting for spring warmth to resume feeding.

funFact: Juniper Geometer caterpillars are masters of disguise — they can stand perfectly still on a twig for hours, holding their bodies rigid at an angle to perfectly mimic a small branch stub, complete with the right color and texture to fool even sharp-eyed birds!
confusionNotes: Many small geometer moths look similar, but finding this one near junipers is a strong clue to its identity. The horizontal wing position when resting helps distinguish it from micro-moths that hold their wings roof-like over their bodies. Remember: if it's small, holds wings flat, and you're near junipers, you've likely found your Juniper Geometer.
contextualKnowledge: What many people call "cedar" trees in New England are actually junipers — true cedars don't naturally grow here. So when you see this moth near those familiar scaly-leaved evergreen shrubs and trees, you're seeing the juniper connection in action, even if locals call them cedars.
compareHints: The Juniper Geometer is the only Patalene species in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other small geometer moths in the region, its close association with junipers and consistent small size help set it apart. Most similar geometers either prefer different host plants or have slightly different wing patterns and resting postures.
